subject: Banking
title: Too Big to Fail
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Too Big to Fail.

hook.text: In 2008, the US government bailed out banks with $700 billion in taxpayer money. They were deemed too big to let fail.

buildup.text: If a systemically important bank collapses, it drags down every bank it trades with.

discovery.text: TARP funds went to Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, Citigroup, and others.

twist.text: Bankers received billions in bonuses the same year taxpayers bailed them out.

climax.text: Too big to fail means profits are private and losses are public.

punchline.text: $700 billion bailout, billions in bonuses. Losses public, profits private.

quiz.question: What is the 'moral hazard' of too-big-to-fail policies?
options: Banks take excessive risks knowing the government will rescue them

details.summary: Too big to fail describes financial institutions so large and interconnected that their collapse would cause catastrophic damage to the entire economy, forcing governments to bail them out regardless of moral hazard concerns.
details.whyItMatters: The too-big-to-fail doctrine creates a perverse incentive where the largest banks take excessive risks knowing taxpayers will absorb the losses. The 2008 bailouts cost hundreds of billions and sparked lasting public anger.
takeaways: Banks deemed systemically important receive implicit government guarantees
The 2008 bailouts used over 700 billion dollars in taxpayer funds
Dodd-Frank imposed stricter capital requirements on systemically important banks

faq.question: Has the too-big-to-fail problem been solved since 2008?
faq.answer: Not entirely. The largest banks are now even larger than in 2008. Higher capital requirements and living wills reduce the risk, but the implicit guarantee persists. If a major bank faced collapse today, the government would likely intervene.

faq.question: Why not just break up the biggest banks?
faq.answer: Political resistance from the banking lobby, arguments about global competitiveness, and the complexity of unwinding interconnected operations have prevented breakups. Some economists still advocate for size caps, but it remains politically infeasible.
